newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia coffee fed has mixed reviews at milestone.
newsitem.headline: Colombia coffee fed has mixed reviews at milestone.

text.p: BOGOTA, June 25 Reuter - Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation is gearing up to celebrate the 70th anniversary of its creation amid both praise and criticism of its work.

The federation, the maximum authority in the Colombian coffee industry, started life as a trade association but is now responsible for managing key areas of national coffee policy -- leading some critics to refer to it as the government's "Ministry for Coffee".
"The federation is a Ministry for Coffee which bows to whatever the government of the day says," said Jorge Enrique Robledo, a leader of the Unidad Cafetera Nacional (UCN).
The UCN is a loosely-woven pressure group of coffee growers, with a presence in nine provinces. It has long been critical of many of the federation's policies which it says has crippled the sector.
The federation currently represents more than 247,700 coffee growers, who together account for more than 95 percent of national production.
One of its most important roles is that of administering the so-called National Coffee Fund, under contract from the government.

The fund offers a guaranteed price to growers for all Colombian coffee and uses the profits from international bean sales for agricultural research, infrastructure and social development projects in coffee growing regions.

In an effort to boost the returns from coffee sales, the federation invests part of the earnings in a network of companies which together make up the Grupo Cafetero, which includes shares in an airline, a shipping company, banks and savings banks.

The multiple functions of the federation as a trade association, policy body and fund manager, has led to what Robledo dubbed a "triple personality". He did recognize, however, that the federation, through its administration of the National Coffee Fund, had played a vital role in providing stable prices to Colombian growers.

Mario Gomez, of the National Coffee Growers Committee, paid high praise to the federation, saying: "The quality of life in coffee-growing areas has increased substantially thanks to the role of the federation. You only have to go to the area and see the level of public services, the improvement in crop qualities and the greater number of schools," he said.
The coffee growers' committee is made up of producers, federation chiefs and government representatives, who together map out the joint coffee policies which the federation then administers.

According to the federation's forecasts, it will invest about 179 billion pesos ($179 million) in regional development in 1997. It is precisely the role the federation plays as a quasi-state institution as well as a trade association that has drawn most criticism, Gomez said.
"Some people don't like the fact that the federation has developed into an institution because it has protected producers from the ebbs and flows of speculation," he said.
The image of the Colombian coffee industry, Gomez said, would be seriously undermined if it was not carefully controlled by the federation.
"In other parts of the world the culture of commitment does not exist," Gomez said.

The federation will celebrate its 70th anniversary in Medellin, Colombia's third largest city, on Friday, June 27, in an event attended by federation chief Jorge Cardenas and representatives of the 16 departmental coffee committees.

That will be followed on July 8 with a gala event, also in Medellin, with a list of guest speakers that includes Celsius Lodder, executive director of the International Coffee Organization, Rubens Barbosa, chairman of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries ACPC, Colombia's President Ernesto Samper, Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo, the director general of Nestle Mario Corti and Howard Schultz, head of Starbucks Coffee Co.
